source.title: Sparsity Moves Computation: How FFN Architecture Reshapes Attention in Small Transformers

page_placements.theme: Neuron basis is privileged by the activation function and training; rotation removes unit-level interpretability

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on neuron-level Fourier structure and interpretability, but does not test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common polysemantic neurons are, or any of the specific claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures Fourier concentration as a proxy for task structure in neurons and principal components. These results concern interpretability and representation format, not mixed responses to unrelated inputs or the prevalence of polysemantic neurons. The reported Fourier and accuracy findings are recorded below as related results, not as tests of a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study measures per-neuron Fourier concentration, PCA-subspace concentration and token selectivity in one-layer Transformers on algorithmic tasks. These are related constructs, not rates of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The authors never frame low concentration as polysemanticity. Superposition and privileged-basis work is only discussed briefly in background. No row measures what any version names, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The main conclusion is that sparse MoE routing shifts computation from FFN to attention, driven by sparse partitioning rather than learned routing. A secondary finding is that GLU gating rotates Fourier structure out of the per-neuron basis while preserving it in subspaces. The authors make no claims about polysemantic neuron prevalence.
record.recipe_differences: Uses activation-based Fourier concentration, PCA, linear probes, and a GLU weight-tensor analysis on small algorithmic tasks; it does not use the original neuron-feature visualization or mixed-input analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The representation measure matters: per-neuron Fourier concentration is low for GLU variants, while principal-component concentration is high. The paper also reports SiLU/GELU comparisons as not materially changing its findings.

fits_no_version.finding: On modular addition, GLU variants show low per-neuron Fourier concentration (0.17/0.16) but high top-PC concentration (0.46–0.49), at equal accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multiplicative gating can rotate task structure out of the neuron basis into a low-dimensional subspace in small algorithmic Transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-neuron concentration in the GLU gate (0.360) and up-projection (0.371) stays near FFN (0.443); the product drops to 0.220 (one seed).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The multiplicative interaction itself, not the pre-multiplication components, reduces neuron-level frequency selectivity.

fits_no_version.finding: Weight-based bilinear Fourier concentration (0.38/0.39) exceeds activation-based per-neuron concentration for GLU variants.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-basis activation measures can understate structure visible in weight-space decompositions of GLUs.

fits_no_version.finding: On histogram counting, the fraction of FFN neurons with strict token selectivity is 0.93/0.96 for GLU/MoE-GLU vs 0.33/0.50 for FFN/MoE (Table 10). This opposes the modadd direction; no row records it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Effects of GLU gating on neuron-level selectivity are task-dependent.

record.problems: The evidence uses one-layer Transformers on small algorithmic tasks and measures Fourier concentration rather than polysemanticity or unrelated-input responses. Most results use 5 seeds. Figure 22 and Table 5 report different per-neuron concentration values for GLU-family models, without an explanation in the provided text.

untested.parts: Vision classifiers; no image models studied.
Prevalence of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models; only one-layer toy Transformers on arithmetic and counting, with no unrelated-token measure.
Superposition as the cause; no feature-count vs neuron-count manipulation tied to polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity from initialization or noise without capacity pressure.
Share of polysemantic neurons under different architectures. GLU vs FFN changes Fourier concentration, but that is not a polysemanticity rate. SoLU and convnets are not tested.
Dependence on activation-range or explanation scoring. Neuron vs PCA vs weight-based Fourier measures differ, but not for polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'discusses' label is generous: polysemanticity is never named, and superposition and privileged-basis work are cited only briefly. 'cites_only' would also be defensible. The per-neuron values for GLU-family models differ between Fig. 22 (0.07/0.18) and Tables 5/6 (0.17/0.16) without explanation. Table 10's token-selectivity result is not captured in any row; it is listed under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Image classifiers and unrelated visual inputs, including the InceptionV1 examples.
Transformer language models and polysemantic responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
Whether superposition or feature-to-neuron capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
The share of polysemantic neurons; the paper measures Fourier concentration, not polysemanticity, and does not test SoLU or modern convnets.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature or related offshoots rather than unrelated inputs.
Dependence on activation range or explanation-scoring choices. The paper compares neuron-basis and PCA-subspace measures, not those choices.

relation.reason: The related work discusses privileged bases and superposition (Elhage et al. 2022), and the GLU result is framed against them. The study neither tests nor uses polysemanticity rates.

tranche.reason: Per-neuron Fourier concentration (power at the dominant frequency) is a related but different construct from rates of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The authors frame it as basis rotation, not polysemanticity, so it is fits_no_version.

source_check.notes: All six rows match Fig. 5, Table 5 and Table 6 (one-layer Transformers, (a+b) mod 113, parameter-matched, 5 seeds). Plain MoE also has high top-1 PC concentration (0.49) and FFN has 0.41, so high subspace concentration is not specific to GLU. Low per-neuron concentration is a gating rotation effect, not a measured polysemanticity rate.
